common_name: Exotic Star Amaryllis (White with Green Throat and Pink Star Pattern)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Exotic Star bears white flowers with a green throat and faint pink star-shaped veining radiating through each petal.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Exotic Star bears large, softly colored white flowers touched with a green throat and faint pink star-shaped veining that radiates outward through each petal, a more subtle, refined color pattern than the bold solid reds of many popular amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

common_name: Double Dragon Amaryllis (Fully Double Red-and-White Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Double Dragon bears fully double, ruffled red-and-white flowers with an unusually high petal count, resembling a peony more than a typical amaryllis.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Double Dragon bears fully double, ruffled blooms in bold red streaked and edged with white, with an unusually high petal count that gives each flower a full, peony-like form rather than the simple six-petaled star typical of most amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

common_name: Christmas Gift Amaryllis (Classic Pure White Holiday Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Christmas Gift is a classic pure white amaryllis long popular as a forced holiday container bulb.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Christmas Gift bears large, pure white flowers with a faint green throat, a clean, classic color that has made it one of the most popular amaryllis cultivars for forcing into bloom around the winter holidays, though it performs equally well as a garden or naturalized bulb in zone 8-10. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

common_name: Summer Drummer Allium (Very Tall Late-Summer-Blooming Ornamental Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Summer Drummer is an unusually tall allium reaching up to 6 feet, blooming later in summer than most ornamental onions.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Summer Drummer stands out among ornamental onions for its exceptional height, reaching up to six feet on strong, sturdy stems topped by loose, creamy-white starburst flower heads with a purple-tinted base, blooming later in the season, from midsummer into late summer, than the spring-blooming alliums most gardeners are familiar with. Its towering height and late bloom timing make it a dramatic back-of-border accent that extends the ornamental allium season well past the typical spring display. The dried seed heads persist and add winter interest if left standing. Allium foliage often yellows and dies back before or during bloom, so plant lower companion perennials in front to hide the fading leaves.
